title: Restoring Hearing to Deaf Children at One Ångström: Dual-AAV Otoferlin (Otarmeni / DB-OTO) & Cisplatin Hair-Cell Otoprotection (Pedmark) — One-Ångström atomic walks inside otoferlin C2A (3L9B), AAV9 (3UX1) and AAV2 (6IH9) icosahedral capsids, cisplatin-bent DNA (3LPV), and human outer hair cell prestin (7LGU); the DFNB9 newborn OAE screening paradox, dual-AAV split-gene recombination under mMyo15, Fudan Lancet & Nature Medicine trials, AK-OTOF, CHORD NEJM and April 23, 2026 FDA approval of Otarmeni, SIOPEL 6 & ACCL0431 Pedmark 6-hour otoprotection, decibel power and sodium-load math, round-window/LSCC microsurgery, and the GJB2/TMC1/MYO7A frontier

teenKit.tldr: A baby can pass a hospital hearing screen yet be profoundly deaf because standard tests only check the ear's mechanical amplifiers, missing downstream genetic failures in inner hair cell synapses.
teenKit.whyItMatters: Structural pharmacology and breakthrough gene therapies like Otarmeni are rewriting the rules of medicine by successfully delivering working genes to restore hearing in children.
keyTakeaways: Otoacoustic emission (OAE) screenings check whether outer hair cells can physically dance and bounce sound back, but they miss failures in the inner hair cell signaling machinery.
Otoferlin (encoded by the OTOF gene) is the crucial protein that builds ribbon synapses to pass sound signals from inner hair cells to the auditory nerve.
Because the OTOF gene is too massive to fit inside a single viral delivery truck, scientists use a split dual-AAV strategy to stitch two halves together inside the cell.

vocab.meaning: A hearing condition where the outer ear amplifiers work fine, but the signal fails to travel properly to the brain.
A specialized molecular docking station that releases chemical messengers at lightning speed from inner hair cells to nerves.
A clever delivery method that splits a giant gene into two halves, packages them into separate harmless viruses, and recombines them inside the target cell.
The use of protective agents like sodium thiosulfate to shield a cancer patient's delicate inner ear hair cells from toxic chemotherapy drugs.

quiz.question: Why did the 10-month-old baby pass her newborn hearing screen even though she was profoundly deaf?
options: The hospital equipment was completely broken and printed random results.
Her outer hair cells were healthy and generated acoustic echoes, but her inner hair cell synapses failed to send the signal.
She was only figning deafness to test her parents' reactions.
Her brain had already adapted to filter out all loud noises.
quiz.explanation: Standard screens measure outer hair cell echoes (OAEs), but miss failures deeper in the neural transmission pathway like otoferlin deficiency.

quiz.question: What is the main engineering challenge when trying to use an AAV virus to deliver a replacement OTOF gene?
options: The virus cannot survive inside human body temperature.
The OTOF gene is too physically large to fit inside a single viral capsid packaging limit.
The virus attacks the brain instead of the inner ear.
Gene therapy only works on adult cells, not infant cells.
quiz.explanation: The otoferlin gene exceeds the standard 4.7-kilobase cargo capacity of adeno-associated viruses, requiring a split dual-AAV delivery workaround.

quiz.question: How does Pedmark (sodium thiosulfate) protect children from cisplatin-induced hearing loss without ruining cancer treatment?
options: It neutralizes the tumor directly while ignoring the ears.
It is injected directly into the brain to block all sound permanently.
It is timed to be administered precisely six hours after cisplatin, giving the chemo time to kill tumor cells before being cleared from the ear.
It coats the outside of the skull in a protective mineral shell.
quiz.explanation: Delaying the otoprotective agent by six hours allows cisplatin to wipe out cancer cells first while still protecting vulnerable inner ear hair cells.
